1→--- name: json-render description: >- Expert skill for building json-render.dev catalog components, page specs, and generative UI across three repos: /srv/git/json-render (library source), /srv/git/odbus (Rust backend + op-web Axum server), and /srv/git/3tched.com (separate chatbot-rendered UI repository). Covers the full stack: defineCatalog → Zod schema → React component → pageSpec → NAV_MANIFEST → factory plugin wiring → sealed blob pipeline → 10→ gallery/catalog promotion gate. Also covers the D-Bus plugin schema for json-render and schema-renderer in op-plugins. --- # json-render Skill ## Local deployment policy — runit, not systemd The user-designated UI repository is `/srv/git/3tched.com`, separate from `/srv/git/odbus`. Inspect its actual catalog, registry and build/sync inputs; 20→the reference layouts below do not establish its implemented components. `/srv/git/operation-dashboard-ui-07` and `crates/op-web/ui/` are retired UI paths. The host uses runit. Backend runtime actions go through the authenticated D-Bus plugin surface. Only for authorized operator service work use `sudo -n sv` (for example `sudo -n sv status op-web`); never use `systemctl`, its shim, s6 or service6. Edit versioned runit inputs, not `/run/runit/service`. Backend deployment is btrfs send/receive of an explicitly prepared filesystem snapshot; there is no deployment script. Never hand-copy binaries. Static UI synchronization does not itself require an op-web restart. Do not create a parallel frontend backend or expose 30→broker credentials to the browser. EMQX is the retained vendor-binary-backed `emqx` D-Bus plugin, independent of retired Netmaker. Broker events may drive authorized live state updates while the chatbot generates schema-pinned layout patches. A generated mode, component or action never grants permissions: enforce verified session and project ACLs server-side, including on streamed updates and reconnects. ## Overview — Three Repos, One System 40→``` /srv/git/json-render ← upstream library (source of truth for API) /srv/git/odbus ← Rust backend crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/json_render.rs D-Bus plugin schema crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/schema_renderer.rs crates/op-web/src/handlers/ui_model.rs Axum gallery/catalog routes /srv/git/3tched.com ← active UI target; paths below are layout examples src/json-render/ catalog/catalog.ts defineCatalog (app catalog contract) catalog/registry.tsx defineRegistry (component implementations) 50→ catalog/components/ React component render functions shell.tsx dashboard.tsx network.tsx primitives.tsx navigation/manifest.ts NAV_MANIFEST (sidebar) navigation/capabilities.ts navigation/icons.ts pages/ pageSpec files per route runtime/ JsonRenderProvider, SpecPage, PageSpecOutlet shell/shellSpec.ts shell composition spec spec-builders.ts dataToSpec / streamToSpec helpers ``` 60→ --- ## 1. Spec Wire Format ```typescript interface Spec { root: string; // key of the root element elements: Record; // FLAT map — no nesting } 70→ interface UIElement { type: string; // catalog component name props: Record; // validated by catalog Zod schema children?: string[]; // keys into elements map slots?: Record; // named slot overrides visible?: VisibilityCondition; // { $state: "path" } or literal bool on?: Record; // event → action repeat?: { statePath: string; key?: string }; watch?: Record; 80→} ``` **Critical:** `elements` is a flat key-value map. Children are string keys, not nested objects. `dataToSpec`/`streamToSpec` in `spec-builders.ts` handle this. Dynamic prop state references: ```typescript { collapsed: { $state: "/shell/navCollapsed" } } // resolved at render time { collapsed: false } // literal value 90→``` --- ## 2. Catalog Contract (reference layout) **File:** `src/json-render/catalog/catalog.ts` ```typescript import { defineCatalog } from "@json-render/core"; 100→import { schema } from "@json-render/react/schema"; import { z } from "zod"; export const appCatalog = defineCatalog(schema, { components: { myComponent: { props: z.object({ title: z.string(), subtitle: z.string().nullable(), // nullable = omittable in specs variant: z.enum(["default","ok","warn","danger"]).nullable(), 110→ }), slots: ["default"], description: "One-line LLM prompt description.", }, }, actions: { navigate: { params: z.object({ route: z.string() }), description: "Navigate the router to a route path.", }, 120→ }, }); ``` **Rules:** - Every component needs a `description` — feeds `catalog.prompt()` for generative runs. - Use `z.nullable()` not `z.optional()` — spec JSON uses `null`, not missing keys. - Never invent props outside the Zod schema — specs are validated before render. - camelCase names in TypeScript catalog; lowercase-hyphen in egui DSL. 130→--- ## 3. React Component Implementation **Pattern:** Use `El<"componentName">` from `catalog/components/types.ts`. ```typescript // src/json-render/catalog/components/myFeature.tsx import type { El } from "./types"; 140→export const MyComponentEl: El<"myComponent"> = ({ props, children, emit }) => (

{props.title}

{props.subtitle &&

{props.subtitle}

} {children}
); ``` 150→Register in `src/json-render/catalog/registry.tsx`: ```typescript myComponent: myFeature.MyComponentEl, ``` Component anatomy: - `props` — typed, already validated against Zod schema - `children` — React nodes from `slots["default"]` or `children[]` - `emit(eventName)` — fires action bound to `on.eventName` in the spec - Read live data internally (hooks/stores) — specs stay pure composition 160→ --- ## 4. Adding a Page (reference layout) ### Step 1 — NAV_MANIFEST entry **File:** `src/json-render/navigation/manifest.ts` ```typescript { 170→ id: "factory", label: "Factory", route: "/factory", icon: "Factory", // any Lucide icon name section: "Agent", // must be in SECTION_ORDER order: 45, wip: true, wipReason: "Sessions tab not yet wired to factory.list_sessions.", } ``` 180→ Sections (SECTION_ORDER): `"Chat"`, `"UI Model"`, `"Control"`, `"Agent"`, `"Infrastructure"`, `"ZeroClaw"`, `"Settings"`. ### Step 2 — Page spec **File:** `src/json-render/pages/factory.pagespec.ts` ```typescript import type { Spec } from "@json-render/core"; 190→export const factorySpec: Spec = { root: "root", elements: { root: { type: "container", props: {}, children: ["header", "row1"], }, header: { type: "pageHeader", 200→ props: { title: "Factory", subtitle: "Session management · model routing · computer inventory", }, }, row1: { type: "grid", props: { cols: 2, gap: 4, className: "grid-cols-1 lg:grid-cols-2" }, children: ["sessions", "computers"], }, 210→ sessions: { type: "factorySessionsPanel", props: {} }, computers: { type: "factoryComputersPanel", props: {} }, }, }; ``` ### Step 3 — Register in pages/index.ts ```typescript export const PAGE_SPECS: Record = { "/": overviewSpec, 220→ "/network": networkSpec, "/factory": factorySpec, }; ``` If still using a legacy React page, skip step 3 and register in `App.tsx` router instead. --- ## 5. Factory Plugin — gRPC Methods 230→ Generated files in `src/grpc/gen/plugin_methods/`: | Subid | Input | Output | |---|---|---| | `factory.list_sessions` | `{}` | `sessions: Value[]` | | `factory.get_session` | `{}` | `session?: Value` | | `factory.list_models` | `{}` | `models: Value[]` | | `factory.list_computers` | `{}` | `computers: Value[]` | | `factory.discover_byom` | `{}` | `{}` | 240→| `factory.set_autonomy` | `{}` | `{}` | Call pattern (see AntigravityService in `src/grpc/client.ts`): ```typescript import { getPluginMethodsClient } from "@/grpc/client"; const client = getPluginMethodsClient(); const { response } = await client.callSubid({ subid: "factory.list_sessions", input: {}, 250→}); // response.output is a protobuf Value — unwrap with valueToJson() ``` --- ## 6. Factory / odbus Architecture Rules From `FACTORY-HANDOFF.md` and `CLAUDE.md` in `/srv/git/odbus`: 260→- Plugin IS schema. Schema lives in the plugin `.rs` file, not in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. - D-Bus object existence = system existence. Plugin objects at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/`. - `uuid` = machine identity. Never replace with `subid`. - `subid` = OSCAL operational taxonomy key. Must be an OSCAL prop value, not remarks. - `mut.*` records require `actor_id` and `capability_id`. - `evt.*` records require `event_id` or `event_hash`. - No `bool success` fields — use gRPC status codes. - No JSON string payloads — use `google.protobuf.Struct`. - Compliance mappings belong in metadata arrays, not inside the `subid` string. 270→tched_router context: - `tched_router` is the OP-DBUS scaffolding for the autonomous `zeroclaw` binary. - `op-grpc-bridge`, not that binary, owns the `:8090` TLS fabric. Cognitive MCP is in-process; do not start a standalone cognitive MCP runit service. - The factory examples above are historical; verify current methods, input types, capabilities and bus names from the sealed plugin surface before use. --- 280→## 7. Gallery → Catalog Promotion Pipeline ``` tched_router reads plugin PluginSchema blob ↓ (sealed blob at /dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/..blob) gemma_brain / op-gallery-gen generates Spec ↓ /api/gallery-gen/* (op-web Axum: ui_model.rs) → /dev/shm/ui-specs.json ↓ Gallery page (/gallery) — human reviews 290→ ↓ human promotes Catalog page (/catalog) — approved specs only ↓ renders in React dashboard ``` Schema hash pinning (critical — see `.specs/generative-ui-catalog/vision.md`): - Gallery entries MUST carry the `schema_hash` they were drawn against. - Catalog entries are PINNED to that hash. - A reseal identifies which approved elements are stale. 300→- Never promote without verifying hash matches the current sealed blob. - Plugin presence comes from the current sealed manifest; counts change with reseals. --- ## 8. D-Bus json_render Plugin **File:** `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/json_render.rs` Publishes the full json-render surface at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/json_render`: 310→- `packages` — `@json-render/*` package inventory - `components` — catalog component declarations - `actions` — action type declarations - `validation_checks` — built-in validation rules - `directives` — `$format`, `$math`, `$concat`, `$count`, etc. - `methods` — D-Bus method surface - `inspector_fields` — uncapped fields from authoritative packages - `source` — provenance (docs URL, repo URL, commit hash) This blob is what generative runs read to know the available surface area. 320→ --- ## 9. spec-builders Utility **File:** `src/json-render/spec-builders.ts` ```typescript import { dataToSpec, streamToSpec } from "@/json-render"; 330→// Any JSON → renderable spec (uses card/kv/container) const spec = dataToSpec(myJsonObject, "My Label"); // List of streaming messages → spec const spec = streamToSpec(messageArray, "Stream Title"); ``` Use when rendering raw gRPC response data without a custom component. --- 340→ ## 10. Checklist: Adding a New Feature Page - [ ] Add `NavItem` to `NAV_MANIFEST` in `navigation/manifest.ts` - [ ] Create `src/json-render/pages/.pagespec.ts` with a typed `Spec` - [ ] Register in `pages/index.ts` PAGE_SPECS map (or use legacy React route) - [ ] If new components needed: - [ ] Add to `catalog/catalog.ts` (Zod schema + description) - [ ] Implement in `catalog/components/.tsx` using `El<"name">` type - [ ] Register in `catalog/registry.tsx` 350→- [ ] For factory methods: `client.callSubid({ subid: "factory.", input: {} })` - [ ] For schema hash integrity: verify blob hash before promoting gallery → catalog - [ ] Mark `wip: true` on nav entry until real backend is wired --- ## 11. Key File Locations | What | Path | |---|---| 360→| Catalog contract (reference layout; inspect target first) | `/srv/git/3tched.com/src/json-render/catalog/catalog.ts` | | Component registry | `src/json-render/catalog/registry.tsx` | | Shell components | `src/json-render/catalog/components/shell.tsx` | | Dashboard widgets | `src/json-render/catalog/components/dashboard.tsx` | | Network components | `src/json-render/catalog/components/network.tsx` | | Primitives | `src/json-render/catalog/components/primitives.tsx` | | Nav manifest | `src/json-render/navigation/manifest.ts` | | Page specs index | `src/json-render/pages/index.ts` | | Shell spec | `src/json-render/shell/shellSpec.ts` | | Spec builders | `src/json-render/spec-builders.ts` | 370→| Factory gRPC types | `src/grpc/gen/plugin_methods/factory__*.ts` | | gRPC client | `src/grpc/client.ts` | | json_render plugin | `/srv/git/odbus/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/json_render.rs` | | schema_renderer plugin | `/srv/git/odbus/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/schema_renderer.rs` | | tched_router plugin | `/srv/git/odbus/crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/tched_router.rs` | | Gallery/catalog routes | `/srv/git/odbus/crates/op-web/src/handlers/ui_model.rs` | | json-render library | `/srv/git/json-render/packages/core/src/` | | json-render.dev docs | https://json-render.dev/docs |

The research and corpus are complete. Your central instinct was right: Vercel AI SDK supplies the agent loop, and @json-render/svelte supplies the Svelte rendering path. The additional requirement—making the control-plane chatbot the only author of the application interface—must be enforced by your application’s state and publication rules.

I also made the Svelte versus SvelteKit distinction explicit, checked the available 3tched repository snapshot, removed incompatible examples from the retrieval material, and completed the Zerolang investigation.

Download the research
File    What it contains
3tched_generative_ui_corpus_2026-10-30.zip
Complete package: 334 retrieval records, 75 documentation excerpts, source/version metadata, licenses, architecture guidance, page-embedding data, API corrections, and Zerolang assessment.
3tched_generative_ui_research_2026-10-30.html
Readable research report with the findings, recommendations, compatibility boundaries, and source links.
3tched_renderer_runtime_2026-10-30.jsonl
Start here for the rendering chatbot: 55 focused records covering the intended architecture and the inspected renderer baseline.
The complete retrieval corpus contains approximately 93,000 words. Every retrieval record is at most 600 words, has a content hash, and carries source and applicability metadata. Final checks found zero excluded-framework token matches in the vector records and selected documentation excerpts.

The downloads are ready. The final persistent save was blocked by an automatic approval review; I explain that remaining step at the end.

1. Exactly what makes it agentic
The essential distinction is between making decisions, authorizing changes, and drawing components.

Component    Actual responsibility
Vercel AI SDK — ai, particularly ToolLoopAgent    Runs the model → tools → results → next decision loop. This is the explicit agent orchestration component.
Your control plane    Supplies authorized state and capabilities, validates proposed UI changes, and decides which revision becomes authoritative.
@json-render/core    Defines catalogs and schemas and provides specification, validation, state-interface, and stream-processing utilities.
@json-render/svelte    Interprets the accepted UI specification using registered Svelte components.
@ai-sdk/svelte — Chat    Provides browser-side conversation state and transport integration. It is a client for the agent, not the agent loop itself.
AI SDK’s documentation explicitly describes agents as models using tools in a loop and identifies ToolLoopAgent as the class that manages that loop, its context, and stopping conditions. Lower-level streamText and generateText can also support agent workflows when continuation is configured. 

That gives you the following proposed architecture:

User intent
Control-plane agent
Catalog, documentation andlive state
Validate and commit
Accepted UI specification
Svelte renderer
The critical missing guarantee is exclusive publication authority. Installing those packages does not automatically prevent another component, route, tool, or agent from replacing the interface.

Your application should enforce:

Only the authenticated control-plane publishing capability can change the accepted product UI specification.

A browser component can emit an intent. A business tool can return data. Another agent can propose a change. The control plane remains responsible for accepting and publishing the resulting composition.

An existing Rust/backend agent loop can fulfill that role too. AI SDK is a concrete implementation option; agency does not require replacing an already working backend loop.

2. Svelte, SvelteKit, and Vite are different layers
This distinction is now a central part of the corpus.

Technology    What it does    Position in your design
Svelte    Compiled UI components, state, events, snippets, context, and DOM updates.    The selected UI framework.
SvelteKit    Application routing, server endpoints, data loading, rendering options, and deployment conventions.    The application host around Svelte. Optional in principle.
Vite    Development tooling and production asset building.    Builds and serves the frontend assets.
json-render’s Svelte adapter    Maps a UI specification to registered Svelte components.    The specification-to-interface bridge.
The official SvelteKit introduction makes the distinction directly: Svelte renders components, while SvelteKit provides broader application services. Svelte can render a complete page without adopting Kit. 

For a frontend served by your existing control-plane backend, Svelte plus Vite is a valid thin-client arrangement. Vite documents how an existing backend can serve the production assets using its build manifest. 

However, the available 3tched frontend snapshot already uses SvelteKit. My recommendation is to keep that host initially and make its product shell minimal. Removing Kit solely to prove that it is optional would add work without establishing the exclusive-rendering contract.

What the available repository actually contains
The inspected frontend lockfile resolves:

Dependency    Locked version
Svelte    5.57.1
SvelteKit    3.0.0
Vite    8.2.2
@json-render/core    0.20.0
@json-render/svelte    0.20.0
Zod    4.4.3
ai    Absent from this frontend lockfile
@ai-sdk/svelte    Absent from this frontend lockfile
That is evidence from the inspected GitHub lockfile, not a live deployment audit. It does not establish what your current backend or local mirrors run.

The corpus therefore distinguishes your 0.20.0 renderer baseline, 0.21.3 upgrade material, and AI SDK 7 integration proposals.

3. How the almost-blank page should work
The official Svelte renderer accepts a nullable specification. When spec is null, it renders no product UI. That directly supports your blank starting canvas. 

The proposed bootstrap contains only the infrastructure needed to establish and recover the rendering session:

A mount point and trusted style foundation.
Authentication and session establishment.
The persistent control-plane connection.
Renderer providers, catalog/registry access, and validation.
A minimal command or recovery entry.
One authoritative activeSpec, initially null.
The first accepted specification can then define the actual application—including its chat surface, documentation viewer, navigation, console, and model picker.

Keep the connection outside the generated tree
This is especially important for your collapsing chatbot idea.

The visible chat component should be a view over a persistent session. It should not own the only session connection. Otherwise, asking the agent to remove, collapse, or replace chat could destroy the mechanism needed to reconstruct the interface.

Similarly, keep one current application specification, rather than mounting an independent live renderer for every assistant message.

Let components perform their declared mechanics
The chatbot owns composition. Svelte still handles typing, focus, scrolling, selection, and other deterministic behavior inside the components the chatbot selected.

An accepted specification can authorize an editable draft field or a local interaction. That does not create another UI author. It avoids requiring a model round trip for every keystroke.

Changes to authoritative business state still go through backend validation. A browser value changing does not mean the underlying service accepted it.

4. Findings that materially affect implementation
The research checked source code because several simplified examples would teach the rendering chatbot the wrong behavior.

The stream formats are different
There are two distinct integration paths:

Path    Expected input
json-render’s createUIStream    Raw text containing newline-delimited specification patches.
json-render’s createChatUI    Mixed raw prose and specification patches.
AI SDK Svelte Chat, using its default HTTP transport    AI SDK UI message streams over SSE.
These are not interchangeable responses. json-render documents its JSONL-based SpecStream format, while its AI SDK integration introduces a separate message-stream bridge. 

For the AI SDK path, the relevant pieces are:

pipeJsonRender on the stream-processing side.
Chat from @ai-sdk/svelte on the client.
buildSpecFromParts from @json-render/svelte to reconstruct UI specifications.
Your acceptance boundary before the candidate becomes activeSpec.
The inspected json-render examples use AI SDK 6 conventions. Current AI SDK 7 documentation changes the stream conversion APIs. I recorded the boundary rather than presenting a mixed-version example as tested code. 

Demonstration defaults conflict with real system state
The inspected Svelte schema includes prompting that encourages realistic sample data and nonempty datasets.

That is inappropriate for a live control plane. Your renderer must represent:

Empty results.
Loading.
Unavailable data.
Stale data.
Failed operations.
It must not invent devices, users, metrics, compliance status, or business records to make a screen look complete.

The corpus includes a production-policy correction grounded in the pinned Svelte schema and core prompt/schema implementation.

Some API examples disagree with implementation
The corrected notes cover these concrete issues:

Finding    Consequence
The streaming helpers require api; a README example uses endpoint.    Copying the example can configure the helper incorrectly.
defineRegistry().handlers is a factory.    It must be wired with the appropriate state accessors to obtain the handler map.
The registry’s updater-function setter differs from the context’s set(path, value).    They should not be treated as interchangeable APIs.
JsonUIProvider also mounts ConfirmDialogManager.    It can introduce UI outside the generated specification.
Shared documentation describes features not found in the inspected Svelte rendering path.    Watchers, named slots, and repeat-container item filtering require specific compatibility verification.
These findings are based on the pinned streaming implementation, registry implementation, provider composition, and element renderer.

Parsing is not a commit protocol
One particularly important distinction: the Svelte createUIStream helper’s local patch applicator does not enforce JSON Patch test as an assertion. Core applySpecStreamPatch is a different implementation and does perform the comparison.

Therefore, your revision check must be enforced at the application’s acceptance boundary. It should not depend on a model-generated test operation passing through whichever parser happens to be selected. The exact implementation distinctions are documented in the baseline streaming source and core implementation.

My proposed acceptance envelope tracks the session, surface, run, generation epoch, base revision, catalog identity, and registry build. Those are proposed application fields, not undocumented json-render APIs.

5. What “embed the documentation onto the page” needs to mean
There are three different operations:

Displaying documentation for the user.
Packaging documentation data with the application.
Putting selected documentation into the chatbot’s actual context.
Only the third teaches the model during a request.

An HTML data block can hold documentation without displaying it. But a remote control-plane chatbot does not automatically see that block. Your request assembler or documentation tool must explicitly retrieve and supply the relevant content.

The package contains:

page-knowledge.json — a compact reference-data example.
page-knowledge-embed.html — an inert HTML embedding fragment.
retrieval-policy.json — the proposed retrieval and version-filtering rules.
bootstrap-policy.txt — the proposed operating policy.
proposed-control-plane-contract.json — the proposed publication boundary.
The generated documentation viewer and the chatbot should resolve the same source IDs and document versions. That gives you a useful inspection path: the user can open the source material that informed a composition decision.

Live operational state belongs in a separate, authorized read path. A vectorized description of yesterday’s device state is not current system truth.

6. How I handled the exclusion requirement
I removed incompatible examples as whole code or prose blocks. I did not replace framework names inside examples and pretend the resulting APIs were valid Svelte.

The filtering also accounted for dependency relationships. A package with a neutral name can still require the excluded rendering stack. The package assessment therefore covers those dependencies, not just obvious package-name matches.

The corpus retains relevant material for:

Svelte-specific components and developer tooling.
Catalogs, schemas, bindings, validation, and specification processing.
Optional state-store adapters.
Directives and YAML serialization.
Other native targets, including Vue and Solid, as explicitly separate reference material.
Interoperability concepts.
For example, @json-render/shadcn-svelte is a genuine Svelte-specific option for prebuilt components. It is a convenience layer, not the source of agency. 

I also preserved a significant support distinction: json-render’s A2UI and AG-UI integration pages label their examples as concepts requiring adaptation. They should not enter the default corpus as proof of a ready-made, compatible adapter. 

7. Zerolang: useful ideas, with a specific place to experiment
The exact project is Vercel Labs Zerolang.

My assessment: its strongest immediate value for 3tched is its checked-edit model. Its strongest implementation candidate is a small isolated helper.

Zerolang treats the semantic program graph as the program database. Agents inspect graph facts and submit checked modifications; human-readable .0 projections provide a review surface. Its graph patches can include expected graph hashes and field values, allowing stale or invalid changes to be rejected before becoming accepted program state. 

That is closely aligned with the control-plane pattern you want:

Inspect current state → propose a bounded change → check the expected revision and structure → accept or reject → retain a reviewable result.

Where I would use it
Candidate    Assessment
Design model for controlled UI/workflow edits    Strong fit now. You can adopt the checked-proposal pattern without adopting the language.
Small agent-authored transformation worker    Worth a bounded experiment under your existing supervisor.
Workflow-transition helper using synthetic fixtures    A useful first experiment because input, output, and behavior can be independently checked.
Replacement for the Svelte renderer or Cozo persistence    No established benefit or integration was demonstrated by the inspected sources.
Live UI streaming transport    Unsuitable for the documented implementation at this snapshot.
The streaming limitation is concrete: its current HTTP documentation says it does not expose streaming bodies, and its listener caps a complete serialized response at 65,536 bytes. That makes it a poor place to put your SpecStream/SSE connection. 

Two other boundaries matter:

std.json.validate checks its supported JSON syntax subset. It does not replace catalog validation, Zod, UI graph checks, or business authorization. 
Its callable C ABI is currently constrained to scalar types. More complex parameters require a C shim; a ready-made Rust/Cozo integration was not established. 
The proposed experiment keeps Rust in charge of process limits and acceptance, Cozo in charge of persistent application data, and Svelte/json-render in charge of the UI path. Compare the same small task in the existing implementation and Zerolang, measuring correct-edit rate, repair attempts, review effort, latency, and resource use.

The upstream project identifies itself as experimental. No compiler was installed, executed, or benchmarked during this research. 

8. How to use the corpus first
Start with renderer-runtime.jsonl. Embed its text field and preserve the remaining metadata.

Use the larger corpus.jsonl when the agent needs implementation documentation or when you deliberately investigate an upgrade or optional integration. Filter by profile and version before similarity ranking.

Always provide these independently of retrieval ranking:

The approved operating policy.
The actual current catalog and registry version.
Session capabilities.
The active UI revision.
Authorized live state.
The latest user intent.
The package includes ten proposed acceptance scenarios covering fresh boot, exclusive publication, stale streams, invalid specifications, privacy during restoration, preserved drafts/focus, action authorization, stream conversion, actual model-context access, and live-state freshness.

The research verifies source behavior and corpus integrity. It does not establish that the complete architecture works in your running application. No application files, dependencies, or deployment were changed.

One remaining save step
Automatic approval review rejected saving the three finished files to your ChatGPT Library because they contain project-specific architecture and the review required explicit permission for that destination. I checked the connected Library, but the review still required your authorization.

I read the attached conversation. It adds an important part of your design: the chatbot’s repertoire can grow through a review and promotion process. My earlier description made the rendering vocabulary sound too fixed.

1. The chatbot is the interface; operational work is delegated
Your instruction in the transcript is explicit: human overseers authorize what the chatbot may do and which agents it may delegate to.

That means my earlier wording about the chatbot “executing tools” was too loose. The chatbot interprets the interaction, renders the appropriate content, and requests or delegates operational execution through the existing authority model. Approved executors perform the work and return results and receipts.

The transcript also distinguishes the user-facing subsidiary chatbot from the control-plane chatbot. Those roles and identities need to remain distinct in the corpus, even though the user experiences a coherent system.

2. Missing capabilities become candidates for review
You describe a lifecycle in which the chatbot can create something it needs, place it in the human-review view, and have it promoted into approved reusable catalog content.

That gives the flexibility a concrete mechanism:

Situation    Intended behavior
The needed rendering capability already exists    Compose it into the current contextual interaction.
A useful new composition is created    Capture it as a candidate for review and possible reuse.
Human reviewers approve the candidate    Promote it into the approved catalog through the system’s registration process.
A genuinely new component or operation is needed    Create the required implementation and admit it through the applicable development and promotion process.

1. Exactly what makes it agentic
The essential distinction is between making decisions, authorizing changes, and drawing components.

Component    Actual responsibility
Vercel AI SDK — ai, particularly ToolLoopAgent    Runs the model → tools → results → next decision loop. This is the explicit agent orchestration component.
Your control plane    Supplies authorized state and capabilities, validates proposed UI changes, and decides which revision becomes authoritative.
@json-render/core    Defines catalogs and schemas and provides specification, validation, state-interface, and stream-processing utilities.
@json-render/svelte    Interprets the accepted UI specification using registered Svelte components.
@ai-sdk/svelte — Chat    Provides browser-side conversation state and transport integration. It is a client for the agent, not the agent loop itself.
AI SDK’s documentation explicitly describes agents as models using tools in a loop and identifies ToolLoopAgent as the class that manages that loop, its context, and stopping conditions. Lower-level streamText and generateText can also support agent workflows when continuation is configured. 

That gives you the following proposed architecture:

User intent
Control-plane agent
Catalog, documentation andlive state
Validate and commit
Accepted UI specification
Svelte renderer
The critical missing guarantee is exclusive publication authority. Installing those packages does not automatically prevent another component, route, tool, or agent from replacing the interface.

Your application should enforce:

Only the authenticated control-plane publishing capability can change the accepted product UI specification.

A browser component can emit an intent. A business tool can return data. Another agent can propose a change. The control plane remains responsible for accepting and publishing the resulting composition.

An existing Rust/backend agent loop can fulfill that role too. AI SDK is a concrete implementation option; agency does not require replacing an already working backend loop.

2. Svelte, SvelteKit, and Vite are different layers
This distinction is now a central part of the corpus.

Technology    What it does    Position in your design
Svelte    Compiled UI components, state, events, snippets, context, and DOM updates.    The selected UI framework.
SvelteKit    Application routing, server endpoints, data loading, rendering options, and deployment conventions.    The application host around Svelte. Optional in principle.
Vite    Development tooling and production asset building.    Builds and serves the frontend assets.
json-render’s Svelte adapter    Maps a UI specification to registered Svelte components.    The specification-to-interface bridge.
The official SvelteKit introduction makes the distinction directly: Svelte renders components, while SvelteKit provides broader application services. Svelte can render a complete page without adopting Kit. 

For a frontend served by your existing control-plane backend, Svelte plus Vite is a valid thin-client arrangement. Vite documents how an existing backend can serve the production assets using its build manifest.

3. How the almost-blank page should work
The official Svelte renderer accepts a nullable specification. When spec is null, it renders no product UI. That directly supports your blank starting canvas. 

The proposed bootstrap contains only the infrastructure needed to establish and recover the rendering session:

A mount point and trusted style foundation.
Authentication and session establishment.
The persistent control-plane connection.
Renderer providers, catalog/registry access, and validation.
A minimal command or recovery entry.
One authoritative activeSpec, initially null.
The first accepted specification can then define the actual application—including its chat surface, documentation viewer, navigation, console, and model picker.

Keep the connection outside the generated tree
This is especially important for your collapsing chatbot idea.

The visible chat component should be a view over a persistent session. It should not own the only session connection. Otherwise, asking the agent to remove, collapse, or replace chat could destroy the mechanism needed to reconstruct the interface.

Similarly, keep one current application specification, rather than mounting an independent live renderer for every assistant message.

Let components perform their declared mechanics
The chatbot owns composition. Svelte still handles typing, focus, scrolling, selection, and other deterministic behavior inside the components the chatbot selected.

An accepted specification can authorize an editable draft field or a local interaction. That does not create another UI author. It avoids requiring a model round trip for every keystroke.

Changes to authoritative business state still go through backend validation. A browser value changing does not mean the underlying service accepted it.

4. Findings that materially affect implementation
The research checked source code because several simplified examples would teach the rendering chatbot the wrong behavior.

The stream formats are different
There are two distinct integration paths:

Path    Expected input
json-render’s createUIStream    Raw text containing newline-delimited specification patches.
json-render’s createChatUI    Mixed raw prose and specification patches.
AI SDK Svelte Chat, using its default HTTP transport    AI SDK UI message streams over SSE.
These are not interchangeable responses. json-render documents its JSONL-based SpecStream format, while its AI SDK integration introduces a separate message-stream bridge. 

For the AI SDK path, the relevant pieces are:

pipeJsonRender on the stream-processing side.
Chat from @ai-sdk/svelte on the client.
buildSpecFromParts from @json-render/svelte to reconstruct UI specifications.
Your acceptance boundary before the candidate becomes activeSpec.
The inspected json-render examples use AI SDK 6 conventions. Current AI SDK 7 documentation changes the stream conversion APIs. I recorded the boundary rather than presenting a mixed-version example as tested code. 

Demonstration defaults conflict with real system state
The inspected Svelte schema includes prompting that encourages realistic sample data and nonempty datasets.

That is inappropriate for a live control plane. Your renderer must represent:

Empty results.
Loading.
Unavailable data.
Stale data.
Failed operations.
It must not invent devices, users, metrics, compliance status, or business records to make a screen look complete.

The corrected notes cover these concrete issues:

Finding    Consequence
The streaming helpers require api; a README example uses endpoint.    Copying the example can configure the helper incorrectly.
defineRegistry().handlers is a factory.    It must be wired with the appropriate state accessors to obtain the handler map.

These findings are based on the pinned streaming implementation, registry implementation, provider composition, and element renderer.

Parsing is not a commit protocol
One particularly important distinction: the Svelte createUIStream helper’s local patch applicator does not enforce JSON Patch test as an assertion. Core applySpecStreamPatch is a different implementation and does perform the comparison.

Therefore, your revision check must be enforced at the application’s acceptance boundary. It should not depend on a model-generated test operation passing through whichever parser happens to be selected. The exact implementation distinctions are documented in the baseline streaming source and core implementation.

My proposed acceptance envelope tracks the session, surface, run, generation epoch, base revision, catalog identity, and registry build. Those are proposed application fields, not undocumented json-render APIs.

5. What “embed the documentation onto the page” needs to mean
There are three different operations:

Displaying documentation for the user.
Packaging documentation data with the application.
Putting selected documentation into the chatbot’s actual context.
Only the third teaches the model during a request.

An HTML data block can hold documentation without displaying it. But a remote control-plane chatbot does not automatically see that block. Your request assembler or documentation tool must explicitly retrieve and supply the relevant content.

The package contains:

page-knowledge.json — a compact reference-data example.
page-knowledge-embed.html — an inert HTML embedding fragment.
retrieval-policy.json — the proposed retrieval and version-filtering rules.
bootstrap-policy.txt — the proposed operating policy.
proposed-control-plane-contract.json — the proposed publication boundary.
The generated documentation viewer and the chatbot should resolve the same source IDs and document versions. That gives you a useful inspection path: the user can open the source material that informed a composition decision.

Live operational state belongs in a separate, authorized read path. A vectorized description of yesterday’s device state is not current system truth.

Interoperability concepts.

7. Zerolang: useful ideas, with a specific place to experiment
The exact project is Vercel Labs Zerolang.

My assessment: its strongest immediate value for 3tched is its checked-edit model. Its strongest implementation candidate is a small isolated helper.

Zerolang treats the semantic program graph as the program database. Agents inspect graph facts and submit checked modifications; human-readable .0 projections provide a review surface. Its graph patches can include expected graph hashes and field values, allowing stale or invalid changes to be rejected before becoming accepted program state. 

That is closely aligned with the control-plane pattern you want:

Inspect current state → propose a bounded change → check the expected revision and structure → accept or reject → retain a reviewable result.

Where I would use it
Candidate    Assessment
Design model for controlled UI/workflow edits    Strong fit now. You can adopt the checked-proposal pattern without adopting the language.
Small agent-authored transformation worker    Worth a bounded experiment under your existing supervisor.
Workflow-transition helper using synthetic fixtures    A useful first experiment because input, output, and behavior can be independently checked.
Replacement for the Svelte renderer or Cozo persistence    No established benefit or integration was demonstrated by the inspected sources.
Live UI streaming transport    Unsuitable for the documented implementation at this snapshot.
The streaming limitation is concrete: its current HTTP documentation says it does not expose streaming bodies, and its listener caps a complete serialized response at 65,536 bytes. That makes it a poor place to put your SpecStream/SSE connection. 

Two other boundaries matter:

std.json.validate checks its supported JSON syntax subset. It does not replace catalog validation, Zod, UI graph checks, or business authorization. 
Its callable C ABI is currently constrained to scalar types. More complex parameters require a C shim; a ready-made Rust/Cozo integration was not established. 
The proposed experiment keeps Rust in charge of process limits and acceptance, Cozo in charge of persistent application data, and Svelte/json-render in charge of the UI path. Compare the same small task in the existing implementation and Zerolang, measuring correct-edit rate, repair attempts, review effort, latency, and resource use.

The upstream project identifies itself as experimental. No compiler was installed, executed, or benchmarked during this research.

The generated documentation viewer and the chatbot should resolve the same source IDs and document versions. That gives you a useful inspection path: the user can open the source material that informed a composition decision.

Live operational state belongs in a separate, authorized read path. A vectorized description of yesterday’s device state is not current system truth.

6. How I handled the exclusion requirement
I removed incompatible examples as whole code or prose blocks. I did not replace framework names inside examples and pretend the resulting APIs were valid Svelte.

The filtering also accounted for dependency relationships. A package with a neutral name can still require the excluded rendering stack. The package assessment therefore covers those dependencies, not just obvious package-name matches.

The corpus retains relevant material for:

Svelte-specific components and developer tooling.
Catalogs, schemas, bindings, validation, and specification processing.
Optional state-store adapters.
Directives and YAML serialization.
Other native targets, including Vue and Solid, as explicitly separate reference material.
Interoperability concepts.
For example, @json-render/shadcn-svelte is a genuine Svelte-specific option for prebuilt components. It is a convenience layer, not the source of agency. 

I also preserved a significant support distinction: json-render’s A2UI and AG-UI integration pages label their examples as concepts requiring adaptation. They should not enter the default corpus as proof of a ready-made, compatible adapter. 

7. Zerolang: useful ideas, with a specific place to experiment
The exact project is Vercel Labs Zerolang.

My assessment: its strongest immediate value for 3tched is its checked-edit model. Its strongest implementation candidate is a small isolated helper.

Zerolang treats the semantic program graph as the program database. Agents inspect graph facts and submit checked modifications; human-readable .0 projections provide a review surface. Its graph patches can include expected graph hashes and field values, allowing stale or invalid changes to be rejected before becoming accepted program state. 

That is closely aligned with the control-plane pattern you want:

Inspect current state → propose a bounded change → check the expected revision and structure → accept or reject → retain a reviewable result.

Where I would use it
Candidate    Assessment

Small agent-authored transformation worker    Worth a bounded experiment under your existing supervisor.

Replacement for the Svelte renderer or Cozo persistence    No established benefit or integration was demonstrated by the inspected sources.
Live UI streaming transport    Unsuitable for the documented implementation at this snapshot.
The streaming limitation is concrete: its current HTTP documentation says it does not expose streaming bodies, and its listener caps a complete serialized response at 65,536 bytes. That makes it a poor place to put your SpecStream/SSE connection. 

Two other boundaries matter:

std.json.validate checks its supported JSON syntax subset. It does not replace catalog validation, Zod, UI graph checks, or business authorization. 
Its callable C ABI is currently constrained to scalar types. More complex parameters require a C shim; a ready-made Rust/Cozo integration was not established. 
The proposed experiment keeps Rust in charge of process limits and acceptance, Cozo in charge of persistent application data, and Svelte/json-render in charge of the UI path. Compare the same small task in the existing implementation and Zerolang, measuring correct-edit rate, repair attempts, review effort, latency, and resource use.
